newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir hostage reward draws no clues in India.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir hostage reward draws no clues in India.

text.p: Despite the lure of a sizable reward, no one in India has come forward with information about four Western tourists taken hostage in Kashmir in 1995, authorities and diplomats said on Tuesday.

The government of Jammu and Kashmir state in mid-December offered up to one million rupees ($28,000) for specific information about the location of the captive tourists, "in whatever state/condition".

"Nobody has so far responded to our offer of reward for information about the Western hostages," Mohammad Amin Shah, the state police officer in charge of the hostage case, told Reuters in the state's summer capital Srinagar.

The controversial Indian reward was announced a month after the United States offered an unspecified cash payment for any information on the hostages brought forward in Pakistan. It was not known if any information had been provided in Pakistan.

Washington provided the impetus for both reward programmes, which were announced only after protracted talks with the three other governments whose nationals were captured, as well as with New Delhi and Pakistan.
India objected to allowing the United States to offer the reward, and Jammu and Kashmir state finally came forward.
American Donald Hutchings, German Dirk Hasert and Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells were kidnapped by Al-Faran separatist militants in Jammu and Kashmir in July 1995.
One other hostage, American John Childs, escaped, while a sixth, Hans Christian Ostroe of Norway, was found beheaded in August 1995.

Indian negotiators last had contact with Al-Faran guerrillas in November 1995. New Delhi had repeatedly rejected the militants' demand that it release separatists held in Indian jails in exchange for the hostages.

A captured militant later said he believed the four hostages had been killed in December 1995. But last year a lengthy search with sniffer dogs of the forest where he said they had been buried turned up no clues.
Diplomats said they had no verifiable information indicating whether the hostages were dead or alive.
In December, Indian police put up handbills announcing the reward and listing phone and post office box numbers.
Shah said he had put 12 officers on the case. "I was hopeful of getting some breakthrough about the case early, but bad weather and heavy snow have hampered our work," he said.

"The phone numbers given in the posters are monitored 24 hours by three to four men in our office, but so far we have not received a call from anybody about the hostages," he said, adding that no letters had been received.

On Tuesday, Pakistan, which rules one-third of Kashmir and claims the rest, reiterated its demand for the release of the hostages. The call came on the eve of a national day of solidarity when all government offices will be closed to demonstrate support for Kashmiri militants.

Visiting U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South Asian Affairs Robin Raphel said in New Delhi on Tuesday that the hostage-taking had been "a very tragic situation but (we) continue to press the investigations".
